newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: W. European cocoa grinds may fall but demand solid.
newsitem.headline: W. European cocoa grinds may fall but demand solid.

text.p: Western Europe first quarter cocoa grindings, one of the industry's key demand barometers, could well show a decline this year but market analysts say this would not be a true reflection of steady, if not booming, consumption.
"There's no real weakness in demand for European products but the overall grind could easily be lower," one analyst said.
"Demand looks to be okay from eastern Europe and 1996 data showing record chocolate imports into the former Soviet Union were certainly an encouraging sign."

The region's main processors -- the Netherlands, which is also the world's largest, Germany and Britain -- boosted their grindings strongly early on last year, one of the reasons why totals will be difficult to top again in 1997.
The Dutch grind figure is expected to be released on Friday while the German and British figures are likely to be announced next week.
Analysts cited other factors such as a growth in processing at origin -- particularly in the Ivory Coast but also Indonesia and Ghana -- which continue to constrain expansion in Europe.

The fact that the crucial Easter period also fell during the first quarter last year but will be incorporated into second quarter figures this year was also mentioned by analysts as having having a possible dampening effect.
A high first quarter 1996 grind across Europe put Dutch factories on just over 100,000 tonnes, Germany's at nearly 70,000 and the UK's at over 50,000 tonnes, the largest for many years.
"They really were very exceptional figures and unlikely to be matched this time around," another industry source added.
All these totals had eased by the end of the year, dented by factors, which will have carried over into 1997.

Commenting on the decline late last year, trade house E.D. and F. Man said: "This was not a sign of weaker consumption but reflected the fact that higher demand was met from imports of cocoa butter from origin rather than beans processed in western Europe. This trend is likely to continue in 1997."
In the Netherlands for example, one of the smaller grinders last year replaced some of its bean activity with cocoa liquor bought in from processing plants in the Ivory Coast.
This dented the fourth quarter 1996 Dutch grind, leaving it up just 3.90 percent at 97,273 tonnes.
Analysts expect liquor replacement to remove around 4,000 tonnes from the overall Dutch total in the first quarter this year, and it may struggle to match 1996's 100,000 tonnes.
"The main players are grinding slightly more cocoa and have no problems on the sales side," one Dutch industry source said.
"But if we add up all the totals, it may be about the same as last year or even a little lower."

The growing consolidation trend within the global cocoa industry has had a particular effect on Germany, where the grind eased sharply towards the end of last year. Plants in Berlin were closed and other processors moved capacity to Belgium and the Netherlands.
By the end of last year the German total stood at just over 56,000 tonnes, although analysts said there may be a slight increase on this.
"I would be very surprised to see the German grind anywhere near the 70,000 tonne mark, it's much more likely to be nearer 60,000 tonnes," one said.
Britain, which had an extraordinarily high grind this time last year, will almost certainly not be able to match it.
Analysts attributed the massive grind in 1996 to major processor Mars putting extra beans through its Selby plant instead of buying butter, a procedure they reckoned had stopped.
By the fourth quarter, the UK grind had slipped back down to around 45,000 tonnes and analysts said the first quarter 1997 total was likely to be very similar.
--Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
